prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Late winter, almost spring. It's like finding a diamond; now I don't want to leave. I sit in the dirt and put my hands in your tracks. For the first time in a long time I don't doubt. Now I know I always knew you were here. You are the beginning of disclosure, the long-felt presence Suddenly incarnate. Behind me my friend warns, If we see the bear, get into a fetal position. No problem, I tell her, I'm always in a fetal position—I was born in a fetal position. Did you know, she says, the body of a shaved bear looks exactly like a human man? I skip a stone, feel a sudden bloat of grief, then laugh. I ask her, Who would shave a bear? We climb Farther up Rattlesnake Creek, watch winter sun glitter off dark water. No matter how high we go I look higher. Sometimes absence can prove presence. That's not exactly faith, I know. All day, everywhere, I feel you near at hand. There's so much to understand, and everything to prove. Up high the air is thin and hard, roars in the ears like love.

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker explores grief, faith, and the search for an absent presence by following bear tracks with a friend through a late-winter mountain landscape. The encounter suggests that absence can confirm presence, transforming doubt into a fragile but powerful sense of nearness and meaning.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Late, For, Now

outputs.L1:
Late winter, almost spring. It is like finding a diamond; now I do not want to leave. I sit in the dirt and place my hands in your tracks. For the first time in a long while, I do not doubt. Now I know I always knew you were here. You are the beginning of disclosure, the long-felt presence suddenly incarnate.

Behind me, my friend warns, “If we see the bear, get into a fetal position.”

“No problem,” I tell her. “I’m always in a fetal position—I was born in a fetal position.”

“Did you know,” she says, “the body of a shaved bear looks exactly like a human man?”

I skip a stone, feel a sudden bloat of grief, then laugh. I ask her, “Who would shave a bear?”

We climb farther up Rattlesnake Creek and watch the winter sun glitter off the dark water. No matter how high we go, I look higher. Sometimes absence can prove presence. That is not exactly faith, I know. All day, everywhere, I feel you near at hand. There is so much to understand, and everything to prove. Up high, the air is thin and hard, roaring in the ears like love.
outputs.L2:
The end of winter, nearly spring. It feels like stumbling upon a diamond; now leaving is the last thing I want. I lower myself onto the ground and press my hands into the marks you left. For the first time in ages, uncertainty falls away. I understand now that I had always understood you were here. You are the first sign of revelation, the presence long sensed and suddenly given a body.

Behind me, my friend cautions, “If we come across the bear, curl up like a fetus.”

“Fine,” I say. “I’m in that position all the time—I entered the world that way.”

“Did you know,” she asks, “that when a bear is shaved, its body looks just like a human man’s?”

I send a stone skipping, feel grief swell abruptly inside me, and then I laugh.

“Who would shave a bear?” I ask.

We keep ascending along Rattlesnake Creek and watch the winter sunlight flash on the black water. However far upward we climb, my eyes keep searching beyond us. Sometimes what is missing can be evidence of what exists. I realize that isn’t quite the same as faith. All day, in every place, I sense you close by. There is so much that needs to be understood, and everything still waiting to be proven. Higher up, the air grows sharp and thin, thundering in the ears like love.
outputs.L3:
In the late-winter landscape, the speaker discovers a renewed sense of certainty and presence. The world around her is still cold and sparse, shaped by snow, mud, and the muted colors of the season, yet it feels newly alive. What might otherwise seem empty or dormant becomes charged with meaning. The landscape does not simply surround her; it speaks to her, offering signs that something real and powerful is near.

The bear’s tracks become the clearest sign of this presence. They are physical evidence of an animal the speaker may have long imagined, feared, or hoped to encounter, but had not fully known as real in that moment. The tracks transform the bear from an idea into a fact. Even without seeing the animal itself, the marks it leaves behind make its existence undeniable. The bear is absent, yet its passage through the snow or mud gives it a startling immediacy.

As the speaker and her friend discuss the possibility of seeing a bear, their conversation blends fear, humor, and wonder. They joke partly to calm themselves, but the jokes do not erase the seriousness of what they might encounter. The thought of the bear is thrilling because it is dangerous, mysterious, and alive beyond their control. Their laughter becomes a way of approaching something too large to face directly, while their fear sharpens their awareness of the world around them.

Climbing along Rattlesnake Creek, the speaker experiences several emotions at once. Grief, laughter, and longing are not separate feelings but intertwined parts of the same experience. The climb becomes more than a physical journey; it is also an emotional one. The natural world stirs memories and desires, reminding the speaker of what has been lost and what is still yearned for. In the presence of the creek, the tracks, the cold air, and her companion, sorrow and joy exist together.

By the end, the speaker suggests that absence can sometimes reveal presence. The bear is not seen, yet it is felt more intensely because of the signs it has left behind. This idea resembles faith, though the speaker does not present it as simple religious belief. Instead, it is a more uncertain and earthly kind of trust: the sense that what is missing, hidden, or unseen may still shape the world profoundly. The unseen bear becomes a reminder that absence is not always emptiness; sometimes it is another way that presence makes itself known.
outputs.L4:
We followed the bear tracks because there was nothing else to follow.

It was late winter in the mountains, that season when the world seems undecided about whether it means to live or remain buried. Snow still lay in the shadowed hollows and under the black firs, but the ridges had begun to show through in brown ribs of grass and stone. The creek below us had loosened itself from ice and was speaking again, softly at first, then with more confidence where sunlight struck it. My friend walked ahead of me, stopping now and then to point with his pole at the prints pressed into the snow.

They were enormous, each one shaped like a hand that had lost its fingers to myth. The claws made clean marks where the bear had climbed the slope before us. It had come out of the trees, crossed the white meadow, and vanished again into the timber. We saw no bear. Only the evidence of weight, direction, hunger, and life.

I had come to the mountains carrying a grief I did not know how to name without making it smaller. Someone I loved was gone, and yet the world kept offering me forms of continuance: thawing water, birdcall, the resinous smell of pine, the blue shadows lengthening over snow. These things felt almost cruel in their beauty. I wanted silence to answer silence. Instead, everything seemed to insist that absence was not emptiness, that what had vanished might still press upon the world in ways I could not touch directly.

My friend did not say much. That was one of the reasons I had agreed to walk with him. He understood that grief is not helped by cleverness. He knew better than to explain loss, or God, or the strange ache of wanting to believe in a presence precisely when presence has become impossible. He simply followed the tracks, and I followed him.

At times the prints disappeared where the snow had melted from exposed rock. Then we would stand still, scanning the ground until we found them again in a patch of shade or soft mud. Each recovery felt like a small revelation. The bear was absent, but its absence had shape. It had passed here. It had leaned its body into the mountain. It had displaced snow, crushed grass, darkened the thawing earth. We knew it not by sight, but by the marks it left behind.

I began to think that faith might be something like this: not the sudden appearance of what we long for, not certainty standing in full view, but the patience to read the ground. A pressure in the snow. A broken branch. A warmth imagined from an imprint. Perhaps the holy does not always arrive as vision. Perhaps it is more often encountered as trace, as disturbance, as the sense that something immense has moved near us and gone on ahead.

For a long time, I had thought doubt was the opposite of faith. Now, walking through that late-winter brightness, I wondered if doubt was simply the snowfield across which faith had to learn to track. Doubt made me look harder. It made me notice what easy belief might have overlooked. It sharpened my attention to absence, and in that attention absence became strangely full.

We reached a rise where the bear’s trail entered a stand of dark spruce. Beyond the trees the mountain lifted into cloud, the upper slopes hidden from us. My friend stopped and looked back. Neither of us spoke. There was no need to go farther. The bear was somewhere beyond our seeing, or perhaps already miles away. Still, the prints remained at our feet, undeniable and temporary, already softening at the edges in the afternoon thaw.

I stood there thinking of the one I had lost. I could not summon them back. I could not make grief into proof of anything. But I could feel, with a force that frightened me, that love had left tracks. In me, in others, in the altered path of every day since their leaving, there were marks of a life that had passed through and changed the ground.

The mountain air grew colder as the sun dropped. We turned back the way we had come, following our own footprints now beside the bear’s. The valley below had begun to fill with shadow, but the high snow still held the light. For the first time in many months, I did not feel comfort exactly. Comfort was too large a word, too finished. What I felt was nearer to being accompanied.

The bear remained unseen. The dead remained dead. God, if God was there, did not step out from behind the trees and answer me. Yet the absence itself seemed to tremble with meaning. What was missing had not become nothing. What was unseen could still be near. And in the fragile evidence left behind—in tracks, in memory, in longing, in love—I found the beginning of a faith I could carry: not certainty, but nearness; not proof, but presence pressed into the snow.
outputs.L5:
It was late, but for now, the city was still awake.

Streetlights glowed softly on empty sidewalks, and the last trains carried tired passengers home. Somewhere, a café owner turned the sign to “closed,” while a student sat by a window, trying to finish one more page before sleep.

Being late can feel like failure, like time has moved ahead without us. But sometimes, late simply means we are still on the way. For every missed chance, there may be another path. For every delay, there may be a lesson.

Now is the only moment we truly have. Not yesterday, not tomorrow—now. Even if we arrive late, we can still begin. We can still speak, change, learn, forgive, and try again.

It may be late, but for now, there is still time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about hiking near Rattlesnake Creek in late winter, finding bear tracks, and feeling an absent beloved or presence become almost real.
counterfactuals.output:
By Rattlesnake Creek the last snow unstitched itself from the shadows, loosening in blue seams beneath the firs. Late winter held the hills in both hands—one cold, one warming—and everywhere the earth was beginning to remember its body: black root, wet stone, the shy green tongue of moss speaking from the thaw.

I followed the creek upstream, where it hurried over gravel with a glassy, urgent voice. The trail was half mud, half ice. My breath came and went like a small weather. Now and then the sun broke through and touched the water, and the whole ravine flashed as if a door had opened somewhere I could not see.

Then the tracks appeared.

Bear tracks, printed deep along the bank: five toes, the wide pad, the slow authority of weight. They crossed the trail and vanished into willows still bare as bone. I stood beside them a long while, as if before a sentence written in a language older than speech. Something large had passed this way in the night, risen from a den of dreams, hungry and real, carrying its dark life through the melting world.

And then I felt you.

Not as memory exactly, not the old ache with its familiar hands, but nearer—like warmth left in a room, like the pause after a name is spoken. You were in the creek’s bright clatter, in the raven knocking loose a shard of sky from the cedar top, in the damp mineral smell of thawing ground. I almost turned to answer you. I almost saw your sleeve between the trees.

The bear had gone ahead into the brush, but your absence moved beside me, heavier than shadow, tender as breath. For a moment the world thinned: snow, water, mud, the prints of a waking animal, and the shape of you gathered from light and cold until presence and longing were one creature.

I walked on carefully, placing my boots beside the bear’s great steps, while Rattlesnake Creek sang over stone. Behind me the trail filled slowly with sun. Ahead, the willows trembled though there was no wind, and I knew—almost knew—that if I reached out my hand, something would meet it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary nature poem in first person that blends grief, humor, faith, and the uncanny; include a friend giving advice about bears and the line about a shaved bear looking like a human man.
counterfactuals.output:
I walk the ridge because the ridge keeps walking,  
green spine under the weather’s gray shirt,  
and because grief, if left alone indoors,  
starts reorganizing the knives.

My friend texts: **Make noise for bears.**  
Then: **Don’t run. Don’t look delicious.**  
Then, after a minute: **Honestly, if it’s black, fight back,  
if it’s brown, lie down,  
if it’s white, goodnight.**  
I send a thumbs-up, which feels  
like signing a waiver with a tiny blue hand.

The ferns are doing their ancient paperwork.  
Moss climbs the dead log with the patience  
of a congregation. Somewhere a raven coughs  
like a smoker pretending to be an omen.

I have been praying again, badly—  
not kneeling, exactly, more like leaning  
into the possibility that someone is home  
behind the bright, unanswering door of the sky.  
Lord, I say, and the word surprises me  
by not breaking in my mouth.

My mother is still dead.  
This is the fact that follows me  
more faithfully than any dog.  
I tell it to the pines. They receive it  
with their usual wooden discretion.

At the creek, light trembles on the stones  
like a creature trying to become language.  
I laugh because my boot fills with water,  
because the body is so committed  
to slapstick even at the edge of the abyss.  
A squirrel scolds me as if I have mishandled  
the entire century.

Then something moves in the brush—  
a black shoulder, a breathing shadow,  
the forest briefly assembling itself  
into an animal.

I remember my friend’s advice and begin singing  
the only hymn I know all the words to,  
except I don’t know all the words,  
so it becomes half “Amazing Grace,”  
half grocery list, half panic math.

The bear lifts its head.  
Its eyes are small and solemn,  
like buttons on a coat worn by God  
while taking out the trash.

I think, absurdly,  
a shaved bear looking like a human man,  
and the thought is so awful and tender  
I almost apologize to both species.

The bear sniffs, decides I am not news,  
not fruit, not a theology worth testing,  
and turns away, carrying its dark fur  
through the understory like night  
remembering where it parked.

Afterward the world is the same  
but not the same.  
The creek keeps reciting silver.  
The ferns keep signing their green petitions.  
My wet sock makes a small obscene sound  
with every step.

I say thank you to no one visible.  
I say it again, just in case.  
Above me, the clouds part a little—  
not enough to prove anything,  
but enough to make the leaves shine  
as if each one had briefly forgiven  
the light for leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic vignette set in the mountains just before spring, where the speaker follows animal tracks and reflects on absence proving presence.
counterfactuals.output:
At the mountain’s shoulder, winter loosens its fist.

The snow is no longer white, but blue with thaw, sugared with pine needles, softened at the edges where stone begins to remember sun. I walk beneath the firs at dusk, following the delicate punctuation of hoofprints—deer, perhaps, or something smaller and more secretive—pressed into the crust and already filling with shadow.

No animal appears.

Only the evidence of passing: a bent blade of grass, a crescent chipped from the ice, the warm dark mouth of a track opening and closing behind me. The forest withholds its bodies. It gives me only their absence, and I learn to read it like a scripture.

Here, the hare wrote itself in leaps.  
Here, the fox stitched hunger through the drifts.  
Here, wings struck snow, then vanished upward.

What is gone is not empty. The valley knows this. The creek under its lid of ice keeps murmuring, though I cannot see it. Buds sleep hard on the alder, green fists hidden in gray sleeves. Even the air carries a rumor of melt, a softness not yet weather, not yet spring.

I kneel beside a track where the snow has taken the shape of a living foot.

It is a hollow, yes—but shaped by weight, by warmth, by the brief insistence of being. Absence, I think, is sometimes the truest proof: the cup left by the lifted hand, the silence after a name, the path made visible only because something has gone on ahead.

Above me, the mountains darken, immense and listening.

I rise and follow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of a fragmented, intimate essay-poem about encountering signs of a bear while hiking with a friend, using the experience as a meditation on longing and belief.
counterfactuals.output:
We knew before we knew.

A stitch of black fur snagged on the splintered bark of a cedar. The log rolled open like a ruined cupboard. Ants stirred in the raw orange wound of it. Your hand went out, not to touch, but to measure the absence.

Here, you said.

As if the bear had only just stepped away. As if we had interrupted a sentence.

The trail was damp from last night’s rain, softened into a language we could almost read. In the mud: a print, broad and caved inward, the claws like small dark moons. We stood over it together, reverent and foolish, two people in expensive socks, holding our breath for an animal already gone.

I wanted to believe in the bear because I wanted to believe in everything that leaves a trace.

The body passing through the world.
The world remembering.

You laughed a little, but quietly. The way people laugh in churches, or around sleeping children. Your face had that look I have seen before and failed to name—hunger, maybe, or recognition. We had been walking for hours. The trees leaned close. Ferns licked the edges of the path. Somewhere water kept saying the same thing over and over to stone.

I thought: longing is also a kind of tracking.

You follow what is no longer there. You kneel in the mud and make a god from pressure. You say, Something stood here. Something heavy. Something with a pulse.

All morning we found pieces of the bear.

Claw marks climbing a trunk.

A berry bush thrashed open.

Scat dark with seeds, steaming in the cold.

Each sign intimate as clothing on the floor. Each one proof and not proof. The bear became larger by not appearing. It expanded into shadow, into the green-black spaces between spruce. It was possible everywhere and visible nowhere.

Isn’t that belief?

Not the thing itself, but the arrangement of the air around its missing.

I didn’t tell you what I was thinking. That I had been lonely in a way that felt prehistoric. That I had carried inside me some vast animal, shy and starving, leaving only evidence: a silence after certain names, the bitten fruit of old hope, the bed turned cold on one side.

You were ahead of me on the trail, ducking beneath a fallen branch. Your backpack was the color of dried blood. Sun moved across your neck in broken coins.

I wanted, briefly and terribly, to be the bear.

To be allowed such density. Such privacy. To be feared and sought after. To vanish into the trees and still be believed in.

We kept walking.

The forest did what forests do: took our noise and softened it. Made us smaller. Gave us mushrooms like ears, stones slick as tongues, a raven’s call tossed once into the gray sky. We spoke less and less, which felt less like silence than consent.

At the ridge, the wind opened everything.

Below us the valley lay in its green weather. Clouds dragged their shadows over the hills. You pointed toward a meadow burnished gold and said, Maybe there.

Maybe there, I repeated.

And for a moment the wanting itself was enough. The not-seeing. The almost. The shared direction of our gaze.

I think of this often now: how we stood beside one another, believing in the same hidden creature. How belief did not require arrival. How the bear, by remaining unseen, belonged to us both equally, completely, and not at all.

Later, descending, we found one last sign.

A place where the grass had been pressed down in a hollow. Warm-looking. Nest-like. The shape of rest.

Neither of us spoke.

I imagined the bear curled there in the dark before dawn, its breath moving the wet blades, its heart beating under all that fur. I imagined it waking, lifting its head, hearing us long before we came near.

Then rising.

Then leaving.

Not fleeing. Not offering itself.

Simply going deeper into what it knew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem that starts with “Late winter, almost spring” and ends with an image of thin mountain air roaring in the ears like love.
counterfactuals.output: Late winter, almost spring, the town loosens its fist around the river and the river, dark with thaw, speaks under the bridges in a language of stones. Snow retreats into the ditches, not defeated but listening, while the first black branches shine with sap’s invisible argument. Everywhere, the world is practicing return: a crow on the chimney, a bulb shouldering through mud, the pale sun touching each window as if asking to be let in. We walk without knowing why we are lighter, carrying our old griefs like coats we may soon unbutton. Above us, the hills keep their blue distance, their old white brows, their silence that is never empty. By evening, the road climbs toward them, and the sky opens cold and bright, and all that has been buried begins to rise in us, weightless and alarming, until there is nothing left but thin mountain air roaring in the ears like love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
